title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 21
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Proving Who You Are
passages.text:
A. The document that now controls international movement began as something close to its opposite: a letter of request, carried by a traveller, asking authorities along a route to allow safe passage and offer assistance. It was a courtesy extended by a ruler to a favoured individual, not a permission the traveller needed, and for most of its history it was neither compulsory nor systematically checked.

B. Free movement across borders was, in fact, the ordinary condition of the nineteenth century in much of the world. Requirements were relaxed as railways made travel common and checking impractical, and several states abolished their documents entirely as relics of an unfree past. The assumption underlying that relaxation was that identity was a matter for the place where a person lived rather than for the boundary they crossed.

C. The reversal came with war, and what was introduced as an emergency measure did not lapse when the emergency did. Wartime controls introduced photographs, standard formats and systematic inspection; the administrative capacity built to enforce them survived, and the states that had built it found the resulting ability to know who was entering and leaving too useful to give up. Temporary controls becoming permanent is among the most reliable patterns in administrative history.

D. Standardisation was necessary and produced its own consequences. International agreement on size, layout and content made documents checkable by officials who could not read the issuing language, which is what allowed inspection to become routine rather than expert. It also made the document a technology in its own right, subject to forgery and to escalating countermeasures, and each countermeasure raised the cost of issuing to those least able to bear it.

E. What the document actually certifies is easily misunderstood. It attests that a state acknowledges the holder as its national and will readmit them; it does not confer a right to enter anywhere else. That structure is why statelessness is so disabling — a person no state will acknowledge is not merely undocumented but has no country obliged to take them — and why the value of a given passport varies so enormously between issuing states.

F. Biometric identification has changed the object more than the principle. A chip storing a facial image or fingerprints shifts verification from a human comparing a photograph to a machine comparing a template, which reduces some errors and creates others, and moves the sensitive material into databases that outlast any journey. The document has become a key to a record held elsewhere, which is a different thing from a letter asking for safe passage.

passages.title: What Hurts and Why
passages.text:
Pain is not a measurement of damage. The intuitive model — that injury sends a signal proportional to harm, and pain is the readout — is wrong in ways that matter clinically. Signals from damaged tissue are heavily modified before they reach awareness, amplified or suppressed by circumstances, expectation and attention, and the resulting experience can be severe with little injury or absent with a great deal of it.

Battlefield and emergency observations made the point long before there was a mechanism to explain it. Soldiers with serious wounds have repeatedly been recorded requesting no pain relief, while people with minor injuries in ordinary settings request a good deal; the difference tracks what the injury means to the person rather than what it consists of. A wound signalling removal from danger and one signalling months of lost work are not the same event to the system doing the processing.

The mechanism now understood involves control exercised from the brain downward on incoming signals rather than only upward from the injury. Pathways descending from the brain can inhibit or facilitate transmission before it is ever registered, which explains why attention increases pain and distraction reduces it, and why an expectation of relief produces measurable reduction through the body's own signalling rather than through suggestion in the dismissive sense.

Persistent pain is where the model matters most, because it behaves as a different condition rather than as a long version of the acute kind. In many cases the original injury has healed and the pain continues, sustained by changes in the nervous system itself — the processing has become more sensitive, and the system is producing pain in response to input that would not previously have produced it. Searching for continuing tissue damage in such cases is often futile and sometimes harmful, since it invites intervention on a structure that is not the problem.

The clinical consequences run against intuition and against patient expectation. Imaging frequently reveals abnormalities in people with no pain at all, so a scan finding in a person who has pain does not establish the cause; rest, once standard, generally prolongs the condition, while graded activity improves it; and explanation of the mechanism itself measurably reduces pain, which is not true of many treatments that cost far more.

The difficulty is that none of this is hearable as anything other than dismissal. A person told their pain involves nervous-system changes rather than continuing damage frequently understands this as being told the pain is imagined, and the distinction — that the pain is entirely real and its cause is not where they expect — is genuinely hard to convey. Clinicians who fail to convey it lose the patient, and the treatments that work are the ones that require the patient's participation.

passages.title: Counting What Cannot Be Seen
passages.text:
A fishery is the standard example of a resource that is destroyed by rational individual behaviour. Fish in open water belong to nobody until caught, so any fish left in the water may simply be taken by someone else, and restraint by one operator produces no benefit to that operator. The outcome is not a failure of understanding — everyone involved can see the stock declining — but a structure in which the sensible individual action and the sensible collective action point in opposite directions.

The management problem is compounded by the difficulty of knowing what is there. Stock size is estimated indirectly, from catch records, survey trawls and age composition, all of which carry substantial uncertainty, and the estimate arrives with a lag. Decisions are therefore made about a quantity nobody has observed, and the political pressure on every such decision runs in one direction, since the cost of a lower quota is immediate and borne by identifiable people while the benefit is delayed and diffuse.

Total catch limits alone produced an unintended and instructive result. Where a fleet shares a single limit, each operator's incentive is to catch as much as possible before the limit is reached, which produced compressed, dangerous seasons, over-capitalised vessels racing for a share, and gluts that collapsed prices. The rule constrained the total and intensified the competition, which is a general property of limits that are not divided.

Allocating shares to individual operators changed that behaviour substantially. An operator holding a defined proportion of the catch has no reason to race, can fish when conditions and prices are favourable, and acquires an interest in the stock's future because the value of the share depends on it. Fisheries managed this way show measurably lower rates of collapse. The distributional consequences are real, however: shares are typically allocated by catch history, concentrate over time as they are traded, and can convert a common resource into a private asset held by fewer and fewer parties.

Bycatch remains the least tractable part of the problem. Gear that catches the target species catches others, and discarding what cannot be landed legally is both wasteful and largely invisible to the statistics that management depends on. Rules requiring everything caught to be landed change the incentive at the point of gear selection rather than at the point of discard, which is the only place the behaviour can actually be altered.

The cases where recovery has occurred share unglamorous features rather than a single policy. Enforcement that is actually carried out, decisions insulated from annual political adjustment, and a fleet small enough that its members can observe one another appear in most recoveries. Where those are absent, no allocation system has been shown to work, which suggests the design of the rule matters less than whether anyone is obliged to follow it.
